nodes.detail: 3 February 1928 — Simon Commission landed Bombay; nationwide hartal, "Go Back Simon" demonstrations with black flags in Calcutta, Lahore, Lucknow, Vijayawada, Poona. Firing in Madras killed one. T. Prakasam bared his chest before armed police. Innovative protests: kite-and-balloon slogans in Lucknow, lorry-alongside-train in Poona. Lathi charges on Nehru and Govind Ballabh Pant in Lucknow. Fatal attack on Lajpat Rai at Lahore 30 Oct 1928.

nodes.label: All-Parties Conference (1928)
nodes.detail: Series of meetings Feb, May, August 1928 — Indian response to Lord Birkenhead's challenge to produce an agreed constitutional scheme. Drafted the Nehru Report under Motilal Nehru as principal author. Rejected separate electorates (kept reservation for Muslim minorities in provinces where they were a minority). Proposed Dominion Status, universal adult suffrage, equal rights for women, dissociation of state from religion.

nodes.label: Jinnah's Fourteen Points (Mar 1929)
nodes.detail: March 1929 — Muhammad Ali Jinnah's response to the Nehru Report's rejection of separate electorates in Muslim-majority provinces. Fourteen demands reiterating separate Muslim electorates, one-third representation in Central Legislature, residuary powers to provinces, federal system with autonomous provinces, separation of Sind from Bombay, full religious liberty, constitutional reforms requiring Muslim consent. Marked Jinnah's shift from "ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity" to explicit communal politics.

nodes.label: Irwin Declaration (Oct 1929)
nodes.detail: 31 October 1929 — Viceroy Lord Irwin, after consultations with Labour PM Ramsay MacDonald, announced that Dominion Status was the "natural issue of India's progress" implicit in the 1917 Declaration. Promised a Round Table Conference after Simon submitted its report. Response: Delhi Manifesto (Nov 1929) demanded RTC be to formulate scheme for Dominion Status, not whether. Failed negotiations with Gandhi 23 Dec 1929 preceded Lahore Congress and Purna Swaraj.

nodes.label: Delhi Manifesto (Nov 1929)
nodes.detail: Nov 1929 — issued by Gandhi, Motilal Nehru, Jinnah, Patel, Sapru and others after Irwin Declaration. Demanded that purpose of Round Table Conference be to frame a Dominion Status constitution, not whether/when to grant it. Also demanded amnesty for political prisoners and predominant Congress representation at the RTC. Rejected by British 5 Nov 1929 House of Lords debate; Irwin told Gandhi on 23 Dec 1929 he could not give the assurance.

nodes.label: Independence Day Pledge (26 Jan 1930)
nodes.detail: 26 January 1930 — first Independence Day, observed simultaneously across Indian villages and towns. Pledge read out in local languages at public meetings; tricolour hoisted. The pledge text (drafted by Gandhi) indicted British rule on political, economic, cultural and spiritual grounds, and committed to non-violent civil disobedience for Poorna Swaraj. Established 26 January as Republic Day of the future Republic of India.

nodes.label: Gandhi's Eleven-Point Ultimatum (Jan 1930)
nodes.detail: 31 January 1930 — Gandhi's 11-point demand sent to Viceroy Irwin before launching CDM. Included: total prohibition, reduction of rupee-sterling ratio, 50% cut in land revenue, abolition of salt tax, halving of military expenditure and civil services salaries, protective tariff for textiles, reservation of coastal shipping for Indians, release of political prisoners except those on violence charges, abolition of CID, arms licenses for self-defence. Ignored by Irwin — led to Salt March.

nodes.label: Dharasana Salt Raid (May 1930)
nodes.detail: 21 May 1930 — 2,000 Satyagrahis led by Sarojini Naidu (first Indian woman Congress president), Imam Saheb (Gandhi's South African comrade), and Manilal Gandhi (Gandhi's son) marched on Dharasana Salt Works. Police rushed with steel-tipped lathis; non-resisting volunteers fell one after another, 320 injured and 2 dead by 11 am. American journalist Webb Miller's report carried image of non-violent heroism worldwide.

nodes.label: Sarojini Naidu
nodes.detail: "Nightingale of India". Poet and orator. President of Indian National Congress 1925 (Kanpur) — first Indian woman Congress president. Led Dharasana Salt Satyagraha 21 May 1930. Jailed during CD and Quit India. Post-independence first woman Governor (United Provinces, 1947-1949).

nodes.label: Khudai Khidmatgars (Red Shirts)
nodes.detail: Non-violent Pashtun movement founded by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan in NWFP ~1929. "Servants of God" — members wore red shirts (Surkhposh). Played major role in CD 1930 — Peshawar uprising 23 April 1930 virtually held the city for a week. Garhwali Rifles troops refused to fire on the unarmed Khudai Khidmatgar crowd. Faced ferocious colonial repression through 1931-32. Ghaffar Khan's mass organisation was non-violent, Gandhian, and Pashtun-national in inspiration.

nodes.label: Garhwali Rifles Refuse to Fire on Peshawar Crowd (April 1930)
nodes.detail: 23-24 April 1930 — during the mass upsurge in Peshawar after arrest of Khudai Khidmatgar leaders, Garhwali Regiment soldiers (Chandra Singh Garhwali led) refused to fire on the unarmed crowd. Unprecedented mutinous act. Court-martialled; Chandra Singh Garhwali and others sentenced to long imprisonment. Symbolic blow to British confidence in Indian troops.

nodes.label: First Round Table Conference (Nov 1930-Jan 1931)
nodes.detail: London, 12 Nov 1930 - 19 Jan 1931. Boycotted by Congress (all leaders in jail). Attended by Princes, Liberals (Sapru, Jayakar, Sastri), Muslim League (Jinnah, Aga Khan, Ali brothers), Hindu Mahasabha (Moonje), Sikhs, Christians, Parsis, Labour representatives, Justice Party (Madras). Princes accepted federal scheme. PM Ramsay MacDonald hinted Congress participation essential — led to Gandhi-Irwin Pact.

nodes.label: No-Rent Campaign in UP (1930-31)
nodes.detail: October-December 1930 — Jawaharlal Nehru got UP Congress Committee to sanction no-rent/no-revenue campaign. Zamindars (loyalists) refused to pay revenue; tenants refused rent. Active in Agra and Rae Bareli. Severe government repression drove peasants into flight. Continued into Jan 1931.

nodes.label: Chowkidara Tax Refusal Movement (Bihar 1930)
nodes.detail: May 1930 onwards — Bihar's contribution to CD since it was land-locked (no salt satyagraha possible). Villagers refused the chowkidara tax (funding rural guards who acted as government spies and zamindari retainers). Chowkidars induced to resign. Centres: Monghyr, Saran, Bhagalpur districts. Bihpur occupation of Congress ashram became flashpoint. Rajendra Prasad injured in lathi charge.

nodes.label: Karachi Congress Session (March 1931)
nodes.detail: 29 March 1931 at Karachi — endorsed Gandhi-Irwin Pact, reiterated Poorna Swaraj goal. Held six days after hanging of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru; black flag demonstrations greeted Gandhi. Passed two landmark resolutions drafted by Gandhi and Nehru: (1) Resolution on Fundamental Rights, and (2) Resolution on National Economic Programme. These remained the basic political-economic programme of Congress.

nodes.label: Karachi Resolution on Fundamental Rights (1931)
nodes.detail: Drafted by Nehru, passed at Karachi 1931. First time Congress defined what Swaraj meant for the masses. Guaranteed: free speech/press/assembly/association, equality before law regardless of caste/creed/sex, state neutrality in religion, universal adult franchise, free compulsory primary education. Economic: substantial reduction of rent and revenue, living wage for workers, limited hours, right to unionise, state ownership/control of key industries, mines, transport. Basis of later Indian Constitution's Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

nodes.label: Second Round Table Conference (Sept-Dec 1931)
nodes.detail: Gandhi as sole Congress representative, sailed 29 August 1931. "Chchello Katoro Jer" (drink this last cup of poison). Hand-picked Indian delegates mostly loyalists, communalists, landlords and princes used by Government to neutralise Gandhi. Winston Churchill opposed negotiating with "seditious fakir". No concessions made. Irwin replaced by Willingdon; Samuel Hoare became Secretary of State. Gandhi returned 28 Dec 1931 empty-handed; CD resumed 4 Jan 1932.

nodes.label: Civil Disobedience Round 2 (1932-34)
nodes.detail: 4 Jan 1932 — government pre-emptive crackdown: Gandhi arrested, ordinances imposing "Civil Martial Law". Congress and allied orgs declared illegal, ashrams seized, peaceful picketers beaten, property confiscated. Over 80,000 Satyagrahis jailed in first four months. At Ras village, Gujarat, non-paying peasants were stripped and whipped publicly. Press action against 109 journalists and 98 presses. Crushed by mid-1932 (convictions fell from 80,000 to 3,047 by August). Formally withdrawn April 1934. Shattered faith in British rule.

nodes.label: Communal Award (Aug 1932)
nodes.detail: 16 August 1932 — British PM Ramsay MacDonald's award allotted separate electorates to Depressed Classes (Scheduled Castes), treating them as distinct minority community (alongside Muslims, Sikhs, Christians). Aimed to divide Hindus politically. Triggered Gandhi's epic fast 20 September 1932; resolved by Poona Pact. Congress opposed separate electorates but pragmatically accepted the rest as it was not willing to change the Award without minority consent.

nodes.label: Gandhi's Epic Fast (Sept 1932)
nodes.detail: 20 September 1932 — Gandhi's fast-unto-death in Yeravada Jail protesting separate electorates for Depressed Classes under Communal Award. "Untouchables remain untouchables in perpetuity" if separated. Massive emotional response — temples, wells thrown open to Depressed Classes across India. Tagore's telegram. Resolved 24 September by Poona Pact negotiated by Malaviya, M.C. Rajah, Ambedkar. Gandhi broke fast 26 September.

nodes.label: Harijan Sewak Sangh (1932)
nodes.detail: Founded September 1932 by Gandhi, with Ghanshyam Das Birla as president and Amritlal Thakkar as secretary, for anti-untouchability work. Gandhi renamed Depressed Classes as "Harijans" ("people of God"). Funds for uplift, temple-entry campaigns, Harijan education. Gandhi's 1933-34 Harijan Tour raised funds for the Sangh.

nodes.label: Gandhi's Harijan Tour (1933-34)
nodes.detail: November 7, 1933 to July 29, 1934 — Gandhi's nine-month "Harijan tour" starting from Wardha. Travelled 20,000+ km by train, car, bullock cart, foot. Collected funds for Harijan Sewak Sangh, propagated removal of untouchability, urged social workers to go to villages for Harijan uplift. Undertook two fasts (8 May, 16 Aug 1933). Attacked by orthodox — bomb thrown 25 June 1934 at Poona on a car believed to carry Gandhi. Temple Entry Bill defeated in Central Legislature Aug 1934.

nodes.label: Satyagraha Ashram, Wardha
nodes.detail: Gandhi's base from 1933 after abandoning Sabarmati Ashram (he vowed in 1930 not to return till Swaraj was won). Also called Sevagram from 1936. Hub of Harijan campaign, constructive programme, nationwide Gandhian network. Gandhi's principal residence until independence.

nodes.label: Poona Bomb Attempt on Gandhi (June 1934)
nodes.detail: 25 June 1934 — bomb thrown on a car believed to be carrying Gandhi during his Harijan tour at Poona; seven people injured but Gandhi unharmed. Orthodox Sanatani Hindus reportedly behind attack; opposed his anti-untouchability campaign. Orthodox accused him of "attacking Hinduism", burned his portraits, published scurrilous leaflets.

nodes.label: Temple Entry Bill Defeated (Aug 1934)
nodes.detail: August 1934 — private member's Temple Entry Bill defeated in Central Legislative Assembly. Orthodox Sanatani Hindus had offered the Government full support against Congress in exchange for blocking this bill — government obliged. Showed limits of Gandhi's anti-untouchability campaign in formal politics and how communalism could be deployed against nationalism.

nodes.label: Vanar Senas + Manjari Senas (1930-31)
nodes.detail: "Monkey armies" — children organised in bands during CD 1930-31 for propaganda, protests, picketing. At one place, girls insisted on their own separate "Manjari Sena" (cat army). Indira Nehru (later Gandhi) led a Vanar Sena in Allahabad. Illustrates mass penetration of CD movement into even the youngest strata of society.

nodes.label: Second CD Withdrawal (April 1934)
nodes.detail: 7 April 1934 — Gandhi announced withdrawal of second Civil Disobedience Movement; Congress Working Committee endorsed. Shifted focus to constructive programme, Harijan work, and preparing for 1935 Act implementation. Critics (Bose, Vithalbhai Patel) called for new leader. Gandhi said "I have no sense of defeat in me... the nation has got energy of which you have no conception".

nodes.label: Communist Party of India (Kanpur 1925)
nodes.detail: Several left-wing and communist groups came together at Kanpur in December 1925 and founded an all-India Communist Party of India (CPI). S.V. Ghate emerged as General Secretary. Called on all members to enroll in Congress, form a strong left-wing, and make the Congress "a more radical mass-based organization". Distinct from the earlier M.N. Roy-led Tashkent CPI (Oct 1920).

nodes.label: Tashkent Communist Party of India (Oct 1920)
nodes.detail: October 1920 — M.N. Roy and six other Indian revolutionaries in exile met at Tashkent and formed a Communist Party of India. Linked to the Communist International. M.N. Roy co-authored the Comintern's policy towards colonies with Lenin. Predecessor (though independent) of the Kanpur CPI 1925.

nodes.label: M.N. Roy
nodes.detail: Manabendra Nath Roy (1887-1954). Founding member of Mexican CP and of Tashkent CPI 1920. Co-formulated Comintern's colonial theses with Lenin. Expelled from Comintern 1929. Returned to India 1930, organised Royist group, then founded Radical Democratic Party (1940). Opposed Quit India, supported war effort against fascism. Later shifted to Radical Humanism.

nodes.label: Kanpur Bolshevik Conspiracy Case (1924)
nodes.detail: 1924 — government trial of early Communists S.A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmed, Nalini Gupta and Shaukat Usmani for conspiring with Soviet Comintern to overthrow British rule. All four sentenced to four years imprisonment. First major colonial strike at the nascent communist movement (preceded the larger Meerut Conspiracy Case 1929).

nodes.label: Peshawar Conspiracy Cases (1922-24)
nodes.detail: 1922-24 — series of prosecutions against Indian revolutionaries ("Muhajirs") returning from Soviet Union and Comintern training at Tashkent Communist University of the Toilers of the East. Five trials, long prison sentences. Aimed to prevent Soviet-trained Communists from organising in India.

nodes.label: Dutt-Bradley Thesis (1936)
nodes.detail: Early 1936 — theoretical and political document by R.P. Dutt and Ben Bradley laying basis for Indian Communists' renewed engagement with Congress following Seventh Comintern Congress (Aug 1935). Held that National Congress could play "a great part and a foremost part in the work of realising the anti-imperialist people's front". Triggered CPI's abandonment of sectarian "bourgeois betrayal" line and re-entry into Congress.

nodes.label: Congress Socialist Party (Oct 1934)
nodes.detail: Formed October 1934 at Bombay during AICC meeting. Leaders: Jayaprakash Narayan (General Secretary), Acharya Narendra Dev (President), Minoo Masani, Achyut Patwardhan, Ashok Mehta, Yusuf Meherally, Sampurnanand. Four propositions: nationalism was necessary stage toward socialism, socialists must work within Congress, they must give national movement a socialist direction, and must organise workers and peasants in class organisations. Played key role in Forward Bloc (1939) and later RSP.

nodes.label: Jayaprakash Narayan
nodes.detail: Founding General Secretary of Congress Socialist Party (Oct 1934). Studied Marxism in the US. Jailed during CD 1932-34. Sensational escape from Hazaribagh jail with comrades in 1942 — went underground during Quit India, organising armed resistance. One of main leaders of 1942 underground. Post-independence: Bhoodan/Sarvodaya leader (1950s-60s), 1974 JP Movement against Indira Gandhi.

nodes.label: Acharya Narendra Dev
nodes.detail: Founding President of Congress Socialist Party (1934). Sanskrit scholar and Buddhist. Principal of Kashi Vidyapith. Pragmatic Marxist; coined the socialist mantra of working within national mainstream: "It would be a suicidal policy for us to cut ourselves off from the national movement that the Congress undoubtedly represents."

nodes.label: Minoo Masani
nodes.detail: Founding member of Congress Socialist Party 1934. Parsi liberal socialist, prolific writer (Our India, Our Growing Human Family). Jailed during CD and Quit India. Later drifted away from socialism; founded Swatantra Party 1959 with Rajaji as right-liberal opposition to Nehruvian socialism.

nodes.label: Forward Bloc (1939)
nodes.detail: Founded 3 May 1939 by Subhas Chandra Bose after he was forced to resign from Congress presidency (following Tripuri crisis). Left bloc within Congress pushing for uncompromising radicalism. Bose became Forward Bloc's first president. Later grew into independent party outside Congress; Bose's exit from India (Jan 1941) to organise INA left the Bloc under Indian leadership (R.S. Ruikar, Aruna Asaf Ali).

nodes.label: "Whither India?" (Nehru 1933)
nodes.detail: October 1933 — Nehru's influential essay answering the question "Where is India headed?" Answered: "to the great human goal of social and economic equality, to the ending of all exploitation of nation by nation and class by class". Marked Nehru's explicit turn to socialism as the direction of the Indian independence struggle.

nodes.label: Lucknow Congress Session (April 1936)
nodes.detail: Nehru presided. Famous Presidential Address committed Congress to socialism: "I am convinced that the only key... lies in socialism... ending of private property... replacement of the profit system". Set tone for Left's attempt to redirect Congress strategy but also began "Struggle vs S-T-S" debate with Gandhian Right wing. Backed by Gandhi despite contrary pressure from C. Rajagopalachari.

nodes.label: Faizpur Congress Session (Dec 1936)
nodes.detail: Annual INC Dec 1936 — first Congress session held in a rural location (Faizpur, Maharashtra). Nehru presided again. Adopted detailed Agrarian Programme. Decision on office acceptance deferred to post-election period. Marked Congress's conscious reach into rural areas.

nodes.label: National Planning Committee (1938)
nodes.detail: Set up in 1938 by Subhas Bose during his Congress presidency (Haripura). Nehru chaired. Drew up plans for post-independence industrialisation and social reconstruction. Included industrialists, scientists, economists. Basis of later Planning Commission (1950). Reflected Left's influence on Congress.

nodes.label: All India States Peoples Conference (Founded 1927; Bombay 1936)
nodes.detail: Founded December 1927 at Bombay to coordinate nationalism in princely states. Reactivated in mid-1930s as major mass organ in states. Nehru presided over Ludhiana session 1939. Led struggles for democratic reforms and accession to independent India. Integrated Indian states' peoples movements with national freedom movement.

nodes.label: All India Students' Federation (1936)
nodes.detail: Founded 12 August 1936 at Lucknow under Nehru's inspiration. First all-India student body spanning the anti-imperialist movement. Led by M.L. Shah. Active in anti-Simon, anti-imperialist agitation, Quit India. Split in 1939 between Left wing (later AISF-CPI affiliated) and Right wing.

nodes.label: All India Progressive Writers' Association (April 1936)
nodes.detail: Founded 9-10 April 1936 at Lucknow. First president: Munshi Premchand. Mulk Raj Anand, Sajjad Zaheer, Ahmed Ali and others were founders. Manifesto drafted in London at Nanking Hotel 1935. Aimed at literature committed to social realism, opposing imperialism and feudalism. Published Urdu-Hindi-English writings. Major force in politicising Indian literature. PWA affiliation overlapped with IPTA and CPI.

nodes.label: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati
nodes.detail: Founding president of All India Kisan Sabha (Lucknow 1936). Bihari saint-revolutionary. Organised Bihar peasantry against zamindari oppression. Wrote extensively on agrarian economics. Aligned with Left. Independent of Congress wings; brought peasant mass politics into the national movement.

nodes.label: Professor N.G. Ranga
nodes.detail: Gogineni Ranga Nayukulu (1900-1995). Peasant leader from Andhra. Co-organiser of All India Kisan Sabha (Lucknow 1936) with Sahajanand. Founding General Secretary. Oxford-educated economist, parliamentarian, prolific writer on agrarian economics. Post-independence: founded Swatantra Party with Rajaji (1959).

nodes.label: 1934 Central Legislative Assembly Elections
nodes.detail: November 1934 — first elections after CD withdrawal. Congress (reverting to Swarajist line under Ansari, Asaf Ali, Satyamurthy, Bhulabhai Desai, B.C. Roy, Rajagopalachari) captured 45 of 75 elected Indian seats in the Central Legislative Assembly. Viceroy Willingdon called it "singularly unfortunate; a great triumph for little Gandhi". Revived Congress-in-legislature as wing of anti-imperialist strategy.

nodes.label: Struggle-Truce-Struggle (S-T-S') Strategy
nodes.detail: Gandhian strategic framework articulated 1934-37. Phases of mass movement alternate with phases of truce/constructive work/constitutional work. Movement phases confront colonial authority; non-confrontational phases work concessions, build cadres, politicise masses. Spirals upward till power transfer. Opposed by Nehru's Struggle-Victory (S-V) alternative of permanent confrontation. S-T-S' was Congress's operating strategy through 1947.

nodes.label: 1937 Provincial Elections
nodes.detail: February 1937 — first elections under Government of India Act 1935 provincial autonomy. Nehru led historic 80,000-km campaign tour addressing 10+ million people. Congress won 716 of 1,161 seats contested. Majority in six provinces: Madras, Bombay, Central Provinces, Orissa, Bihar, UP. Plurality but not majority in Bengal, Assam, NWFP. Massive rejection of 1935 Act's federal side. Prestige of Congress as alternative state soared.

nodes.label: Office Acceptance Debate (1936-37)
nodes.detail: 1936-37 Congress internal debate on whether to form ministries under 1935 Act after election victory. Nehru, Bose, CSP, Communists opposed — called it surrender, co-option. Right wing (Patel, Rajendra Prasad, Rajagopalachari) favoured acceptance as tactical use of colonial framework. Gandhi initially reluctant, warmed up by early 1936. Working Committee ultimately accepted July 1937. Congress formed ministries in 6+2 provinces.

nodes.label: Congress Ministries (July 1937 - Oct 1939)
nodes.detail: Formed July 1937 in Madras, Bombay, CP, Orissa, Bihar, UP; later NWFP and Assam. Lasted 28 months till resignation in October 1939 (over WWII declaration without consultation). Parliamentary Sub-Committee (Patel, Maulana Azad, Rajendra Prasad) coordinated. Ministers reduced own salaries Rs 2000→500. Restored civil liberties, repealed emergency laws, released prisoners, ended press restrictions. Major achievements in agrarian reform, Harijan uplift, prohibition, education.

nodes.label: Parliamentary Sub-Committee (1937)
nodes.detail: Central control board formed by CWC July 1937 to coordinate Congress provincial ministries and prevent British strategy of "provincializing" the Congress. Members: Sardar Patel, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Rajendra Prasad. Ensured Congress Ministries remained answerable to the all-India Working Committee, not to provincial legislatures alone.

nodes.label: Congress Election Manifesto (1936)
nodes.detail: Issued 1936 ahead of 1937 elections. Reaffirmed total rejection of 1935 Act. Promised: restoration of civil liberties, release of political prisoners, removal of disabilities on sex and untouchability, radical agrarian transformation, substantial rent/revenue reduction, rural debt scaling-down, cheap credit, right to form trade unions and strike. Left imprint on manifesto reflected in pro-worker/pro-peasant programme.

nodes.label: CPI Banned (July 1934)
nodes.detail: July 1934 — Government of India declared the Communist Party of India illegal under the Criminal Law Amendment Act. Followed the Meerut Conspiracy Case convictions and CPI's sectarian post-1928 turn. Ban remained during Congress Provincial Ministry era (1937-39) since it was a Central Government order; Congress provinces could not lift it but allowed CPI members to function openly. Legalised only in 1942 (during war alliance with USSR).

nodes.label: Independence for India League (1928)
nodes.detail: Founded 1928 by Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Bose — pressed for complete independence and "a socialist revision of the economic structure of society". Worked within Congress. Helped build momentum toward 1929 Lahore Purna Swaraj resolution. Forerunner of later Left consolidation in Congress.

nodes.label: All India Kisan Sabha (April 1936)
nodes.detail: Originally founded as All-India Kisan Congress at Lucknow April 1936, later renamed AIKS. President: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati (founder of Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha 1929). General Secretary: N.G. Ranga. Adopted Kisan Manifesto which influenced Congress Faizpur Programme 1936. Zamindari abolition slogan adopted 1935. Key leaders: Ram Manohar Lohia, Sohan Singh Josh, Indulal Yagnik, Jayaprakash Narayan. CPI-aligned after 1935 led to split in 1943 (over People's War line).

nodes.label: Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (1929)
nodes.detail: Founded 1929 by Swami Sahajanand Saraswati. First organised peasant body in Bihar. Focus: zamindari abolition, Bakasht lands restoration, end illegal levies. Led major Bakasht land struggles 1938-39. Key leaders: Karyanand Sharma, Rahul Sankritayan, Yadunandan Sharma, Panchanan Sharma. Precursor of AIKS (1936).

nodes.label: Bakasht Lands Struggle (Bihar 1938-39)
nodes.detail: Bakasht lands = tenant lands lost to zamindars during Depression 1929-32 for non-payment, cultivated as share-croppers. Major flashpoint 1938-39 between Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha and Congress Ministry. Yadunandan Sharma won 850/1000 bighas back at Reora, Gaya; Karyanand Sharma led Barahiya-tal Monghyr struggle; Jamuna Karjee Saran; Rahul Sankritayan Annawari. August 1939: ~600 activists arrested. Struggle continued till zamindari abolition.

nodes.label: Tebhaga Movement (Bengal 1946-47)
nodes.detail: Late 1946 — Bengal share-croppers (bargadars) demanded tebhaga (two-thirds share) of crop instead of half paid to jotedars; crops to be stored in bargadar khamars. Led by Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha. Floud Commission had already recommended this. Boosted by Muslim League Suhrawardy Ministry's Bargadars Temporary Regulation Bill (Jan 22, 1947) but the Bill was not pursued. Major clashes, 20 peasants killed at Khanpur. Crushed by Feb 1947. Finally addressed by Congress's Bargadars Act 1950. Centres: Dinajpur, Rangpur, Jalpaiguri, Mymensingh, Midnapore, 24-Parganas. Rajbansi Kshatriya base; spread to Muslims, Hajongs, Santhals, Oraons.

nodes.label: Punnapra-Vayalar Uprising (Oct 1946)
nodes.detail: October 1946 — workers and peasants uprising in coir industry regions of Punnapra and Vayalar, Travancore State. Communist-led. Rose against Dewan Sir C.P. Ramaswamy Aiyar's proposed "American Model" plan for Travancore independence + labour repression. Police shot at workers in Punnapra (22 Oct); Vayalar workers followed (27 Oct). Thousands killed by Travancore State forces. Contributed to Travancore eventually acceding to Indian Union.

nodes.label: Telangana Rebellion (1946-51)
nodes.detail: July 1946 — Communist-led peasant uprising in Telangana districts of Hyderabad State against Nizam's rule and feudal landlords (doras), bonded labour (vetti), and forced food procurement. Armed struggle in 4,000 villages; redistributed land, abolished vetti, set up peasant committees. Continued resisting Nizam's Razakars. Indian Army's Hyderabad Police Action (Sept 1948) merged struggle against Nizam with Indian integration. CPI called off armed struggle 1951.

nodes.label: Bengal Famine (1943)
nodes.detail: Great Bengal Famine of 1943 killed 2-3 million through starvation, disease and malnutrition. Caused by wartime rice hoarding, Burma rice imports stopping, scorched-earth policy, British diversion of food to war effort, boat-denial policy, and Churchill's refusal to divert Commonwealth shipping. Massive relief work by Kisan Sabha and Communist rank-and-file. Major political scar for last years of British rule. Amartya Sen's "Poverty and Famines" (1981) analysed it as an entitlement failure.

nodes.label: Praja Mandals (States Peoples Conferences)
nodes.detail: States Peoples Conferences/Associations in princely states modelled on the INC. Emerged after 1920 Non-Cooperation impact. Examples: Mysore, Hyderabad, Baroda, Kathiawad States, Deccan States, Jamnagar, Indore, Nawanagar. Culminated in All India States People's Conference December 1927. Demanded responsible government, civil liberties, abolition of feudal levies in states. Nehru presided over Ludhiana AISPC 1939.

nodes.label: Rajkot Satyagraha (1938-39)
nodes.detail: Rajkot (Kathiawad) — protest against Thakore Dharmendrasinhji's misrule and Dewan Virawala's monopolies (on matches, sugar, rice, cinema licences). Lapse of Praja Pratinidhi Sabha and increased taxes provoked mass agitation. Gandhi's personal intervention — his birthplace. Kasturba Gandhi was arrested. Chief Justice Maurice Gwyer arbitrated but Virawala reneged. Became national issue showing Gandhi's direct engagement with princely state politics.

nodes.label: Hyderabad State Congress (1938)
nodes.detail: Founded 1938 — demanded responsible government in Hyderabad under Nizam Osman Ali Khan. Banned soon after. Leaders like Swami Ramananda Tirtha, Govindbhai Shroff led movement. Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (formed 1927) grew into Razakars under Qasim Razvi, organized communal violence against Hindus + anti-integration. Hyderabad refused accession in 1947; Operation Polo (Indian Police Action, 13-17 Sept 1948) integrated the state.

nodes.label: Quit Kashmir Movement (May 1946)
nodes.detail: May 1946 — Sheikh Abdullah's National Conference (renamed from Muslim Conference 1939) launched "Quit Kashmir" against Maharaja Hari Singh, inspired by Congress's Quit India. Sheikh Abdullah arrested. Nehru tried to go to Srinagar to defend him, was arrested at border. Shaped the drama of Kashmir accession in Oct 1947 when Pakistani tribal invasion forced Maharaja to sign Instrument of Accession.

nodes.label: Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah
nodes.detail: "Sher-e-Kashmir". Founded All Jammu and Kashmir Muslim Conference 1932 against Maharaja Hari Singh's autocracy; renamed National Conference 1939 to widen base. Led Quit Kashmir 1946. Friend of Nehru. Became first PM of Jammu & Kashmir (Oct 1947); later deposed (1953) and jailed for decades.

nodes.label: FICCI — Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industry (1927)
nodes.detail: Founded 1927 by G.D. Birla, Purshottamdas Thakurdas and others as national apex of Indian commercial/industrial/financial interests. Saw itself as "national guardians of trade, commerce and industry" performing in the economic sphere what a national government would. Consistently supported Congress (not Liberal Party); boycotted First RTC 1930; pushed for tariff protection, lower sterling ratio, economic autonomy. Later drafted Bombay Plan 1944.

nodes.label: Ghanshyam Das Birla
nodes.detail: Industrialist, Marwari. Co-founder of FICCI (1927). Financial supporter of Congress and Gandhi (Sevagram Ashram built on land he provided). Pushed capitalist support for nationalism while ideologically opposing communism. Negotiated Congress-British compromises in 1930s-40s. Signatory of Bombay Plan 1944. Founder of House of Birla (Hindustan Motors, Grasim, Birla Brothers).

nodes.label: Purshottamdas Thakurdas
nodes.detail: Cotton merchant and financier. Co-founder of FICCI (first President 1927-28). Central architect of Indian capitalist class's political strategy. Co-signatory of Bombay Plan 1944. Moderate but consistent Indian nationalist; rejected Public Safety Bill 1928. Influenced Gandhi-Irwin negotiations 1931.

nodes.label: J.R.D. Tata
nodes.detail: Jehangir Ratanji Dadabhoy Tata. Chairman of Tata Sons 1938-1988. First licensed pilot of India 1929, founded Tata Airlines (1932) → Air India. Signatory of Bombay Plan 1944. Modernising industrialist. Aug 1942 — co-signed with Purshottamdas and Birla letter to Viceroy urging political freedom as only solution before Quit India.

nodes.label: League Against Imperialism (Feb 1927)
nodes.detail: Founded February 1927 at Brussels — anti-colonial international. Congress affiliated as associated member; Nehru elected to Executive Council. Other honorary presidents: Albert Einstein, Romain Rolland, Madame Sun Yat-Sen, George Lansbury. Marked Congress's foreign-policy framework of solidarity with anti-colonial struggles worldwide. Nehru's exposure here shaped his anti-imperialist internationalism.

nodes.label: Congress Foreign Department (1927)
nodes.detail: Opened at INC Calcutta session December 1927 after Nehru's Brussels participation. Developed contacts with foreign anti-imperialist movements. Precursor of Ministry of External Affairs. Built relationships with Ireland, Egypt, China, Burma, Palestine, Soviet Union.

nodes.label: Dr Dwarkanath Kotnis
nodes.detail: Member of Congress medical mission to China (sent 1938 under Dr. M. Atal). Worked with Eighth Route Army under Mao Zedong's command against Japanese invasion. Married Chinese nurse Guo Qinglan. Died 1942 in China. Symbol of India-China anti-imperialist solidarity. V. Shantaram's film "Dr Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani" (1946) popularised his story.

nodes.label: China Day (June 12) + Ethiopia Day (May 9)
nodes.detail: Congress-observed anti-fascist solidarity days: 9 May 1936 as Ethiopia Day (Italian fascist invasion of Ethiopia 1935); 27 September 1936 as Palestine Day (Arab-Jewish British-mandate crisis); 12 June 1938 as China Day (Japanese invasion of China 1937). Pan-colonial solidarity hallmark of Congress foreign policy 1936-39 under Nehru.

nodes.label: Indian Support for Spanish Republic (1936-39)
nodes.detail: Congress strongly supported Spanish Republican government against Franco/fascism. Faizpur Congress Dec 1936 (Nehru presidential address): "our battles are being fought (in Spain)". Nehru with V.K. Krishna Menon visited Republican Spain June 1938, spent 5 days in bombed Barcelona. Gandhi sent message to Juan Negrin. First Indian engagement with European anti-fascist war.

nodes.label: Haripura Congress Session (Feb 1938)
nodes.detail: Feb 1938 — Subhas Chandra Bose elected Congress President for first time. Bose proposed resolution condemning Japanese aggression in China, British approach in Palestine, fascist attacks on Ethiopia/Spain/Czechoslovakia. Set up National Planning Committee under Nehru. Famous "Haripura Panels" by Nandalal Bose — Santiniketan school paintings of Indian rural life for session decor.

nodes.label: Tripuri Crisis (March 1939)
nodes.detail: March 1939 at Tripuri Congress — Subhas Bose re-elected President defeating Gandhi's candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya (1580 vs 1377). Gandhi called it "my defeat". But at Tripuri session, G.B. Pant's resolution (backed by Gandhi) effectively curtailed Bose's powers by requiring him to run the Working Committee as per Gandhi's wishes. Socialists refused to back Bose; CSP abstained. Bose resigned April 1939, founded Forward Bloc 3 May 1939. Key rupture in the Left-Right dynamic.

nodes.label: V.K. Krishna Menon
nodes.detail: Kerala-born intellectual, lawyer, Marxist. Secretary of India League London from 1930. Key propagandist of Indian independence in Britain. Edited Pelican Books. Close friend of Nehru; accompanied Nehru to Republican Spain June 1938. Post-independence: Defence Minister (1957-62), resigned after 1962 India-China war.

nodes.label: Munich Agreement & Congress Response (Sept 1938)
nodes.detail: 29-30 September 1938 — Britain and France abandoned Czechoslovakia to Nazi Germany. CWC (in Nehru's absence) passed resolution of grave concern. Gandhi in Harijan: "working committee wrung itself with pain while their doom was being decided". Nehru (then in Europe) refused to visit Germany as state guest, went to Prague instead. Called Munich "the rape of Czechoslovakia with England and France holding her forcibly down". At Tripuri 1939, Congress officially dissociated from British foreign policy. Triggered Congress's anti-fascist + anti-imperialist stance before WWII.

nodes.label: Communalism (Definition & Three Stages)
nodes.detail: Bipin Chandra's analytical framework: Communal ideology has three stages. (1) Belief that people following the same religion have common secular (political/economic/social) interests; (2) Belief that their interests differ from those of other religious communities; (3) Belief that their interests are mutually hostile and antagonistic. Each stage leads to the next unless actively countered. Jinnah's trajectory from "Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity" to Pakistan demand illustrates this sliding logic.

nodes.label: Extreme Communalism (1937 onwards)
nodes.detail: Post-1937 fascist-style phase of communalism. Motifs of domination/suppression/extermination became mainstream propaganda. Fear-and-hatred based; targeted co-religionists among nationalists. Mass-mobilizing unlike earlier elite/liberal phase. Drivers: Congress 1937 electoral dominance pushed landlords/zamindars to communal parties; Congress 1937 expelled communalists from its membership; fascist mass-politics model became available. WWII (Sept 1939) allowed colonial rulers to recognise League as sole spokesperson for Muslims.

nodes.label: Muslim Mass Contact Programme (1937)
nodes.detail: Launched by Nehru and the Congress in 1937 after the party's huge election victory. Aimed to take Congress's secular nationalist programme directly to Muslim masses, bypassing Muslim League. Alarmed Jinnah and accelerated League's shift to extreme communalism and separatism. Programme itself was undermined by WWII and Congress ministries' resignation Oct 1939.

nodes.label: Muslim League Revival under Jinnah (1936)
nodes.detail: Jinnah returned from London 1935 and revived the moribund Muslim League. Initially attempted liberal-communal line — stressed Indian nationalism and Hindu-Muslim cooperation. League fought 1937 elections on semi-nationalist Congress-type programme (only Muslim demands: Urdu/script protection, amelioration of Muslim conditions). Won only 109 of 482 reserved Muslim seats (4.8% of Muslim vote). Post-defeat pivot to mass communal politics.

nodes.label: Hindu Mahasabha
nodes.detail: Founded 1915 by Madan Mohan Malaviya and Lala Lajpat Rai at Haridwar; revived 1923. Key liberal-communal Hindu platform in 1920s. Fared poorly in 1937 elections. Under V.D. Savarkar's presidency (1937-42), shifted to fascist-style extreme communalism — "Hindus are already reduced to veritable helots throughout our land". Key arena for Hindu communal politics in 1930s-40s.

nodes.label: V.D. Savarkar
nodes.detail: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar (1883-1966). Early revolutionary leader (Indian War of Independence 1909). Wrote "Essentials of Hindutva" (1923) — founding text of Hindu nationalism; defined Hindutva as cultural-racial unity distinct from religion. President of Hindu Mahasabha 1937-42. Coined two-nation theory for Hindus before Jinnah did for Muslims. Tried (and acquitted) in Gandhi assassination 1948.

nodes.label: Hindutva (Savarkar, 1923)
nodes.detail: Concept articulated by V.D. Savarkar in his 1923 book "Essentials of Hindutva" (later published as "Hindutva: Who is a Hindu?"). Defined Hindu as anyone with pitribhu (fatherland) and punyabhu (holy land) both in India — excluding Muslims and Christians whose punyabhu lay in Arabia/Palestine. Foundational text of Hindu nationalism. Distinguished "Hindutva" (Hindu-ness, cultural) from "Hinduism" (religion).

nodes.label: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS, 1925)
nodes.detail: Founded Vijayadashami 27 September 1925 at Nagpur by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar. Cadre-based Hindu nationalist organisation on fascist-inspired organisational lines (daily shakhas, paramilitary drills, uniform). Maharashtra base until 1930s, branched out under M.S. Golwalkar. Role during Partition: organised Hindu-Sikh resistance in Punjab. Banned briefly after Gandhi's assassination Jan 1948 — Nathuram Godse was an ex-member.

nodes.label: K.B. Hedgewar
nodes.detail: Keshav Baliram Hedgewar (1889-1940). Nagpur-based physician. Active in Tilak's Home Rule League and INC in 1920s (participated in Non-Cooperation). Founded RSS on Vijayadashami 27 September 1925. Emphasised character-building, physical drills, Hindu cultural unity. Died 21 June 1940 in Nagpur; Golwalkar succeeded him.

nodes.label: M.S. Golwalkar (Guruji)
nodes.detail: Madhav Sadashiv Golwalkar (1906-1973). Second Sarsanghchalak (supreme chief) of RSS from 1940 till 1973. Codified RSS ideology in his 1939 booklet "We, or Our Nationhood Defined". Articulated supremacist Hindu nationalism — non-Hindu peoples must adopt Hindu culture or live "wholly subordinated to the Hindu nation, claiming nothing, deserving no privileges". Praised Nazi Germany's "race spirit" resurgence.

nodes.label: "We, Or Our Nationhood Defined" (Golwalkar, 1939)
nodes.detail: 1939 booklet by M.S. Golwalkar codifying extreme Hindu nationalism. Advocated: non-Hindus must adopt Hindu culture/language/religion or stay "wholly subordinated to the Hindu nation, claiming nothing, deserving no privileges, far less any preferential treatment — not even citizen's rights". Praised Italy and Germany for their "race spirit" revival. Foundational doctrine of RSS extremism in 1940s.

nodes.label: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
nodes.detail: Islamic scholar, journalist (Al-Hilal, Al-Balagh), nationalist. Prominent Khilafat leader. Youngest Congress President at 35 (1923), and its longest-serving (Congress President Sept 1939 to Feb 1946 — through Quit India, Simla Conference, Cabinet Mission). Consistent opponent of Partition and Muslim separatism. Branded by League propaganda as Congress's "show boy". Post-independence first Education Minister.

nodes.label: Great Calcutta Killing (Aug 1946)
nodes.detail: 16-19 August 1946 — communal violence after Muslim League's Direct Action Day call. ~4,000-5,000 killed in 72-96 hours in Calcutta. Rioting started Muslims attacking Hindus, Hindus retaliating. Fazl-ul-Huq's successor Suhrawardy's Muslim League Ministry refused to contain violence. Broke civil-political unity that had held 1920-46. Cascade effect — Noakhali riots (Oct), Bihar (Oct-Nov), UP/Punjab 1947. Final push toward Partition.

nodes.label: Bihar Communal Riots (Oct-Nov 1946)
nodes.detail: October-November 1946 — large-scale massacre of Muslims in Chhapra, Saran, Patna in retaliation for Noakhali violence. Estimated 5,000-8,000 dead (far higher than Noakhali deaths). Gandhi reached Bihar early Nov and began his walking mission to restore peace. Turned Gandhi's full focus to intercommunal violence at precisely the moment partition politics was being negotiated.

nodes.label: A.K. Fazlul Huq
nodes.detail: Abul Kasem Fazlul Huq — Bengali politician. Krishak Praja Party leader. Premier of Bengal 1937-43 in coalition. Moved the Lahore Resolution 23 March 1940. Later distanced from Jinnah, formed progressive coalition 1941. Rejoined League, removed as Premier 1943 during Bengal Famine. Shifted to parliamentary politics after independence (Pakistan, then East Pakistan).

nodes.label: Unionist Party (Punjab)
nodes.detail: Non-communal cross-community agrarian party of Punjab big landlords, formed 1923 by Fazl-e-Hussain. Ruled Punjab through 1937 and 1946 elections. Multi-confessional alliance of Muslim Unionists + Jat Sikhs + Hindu Jats. Declined 1946 as Muslim landlords switched to Muslim League under pressure. Broke during Partition. Model of non-communal provincial politics before 1946.

nodes.label: Muhammad Iqbal
nodes.detail: Allama Iqbal (1877-1938). Urdu-Persian poet-philosopher. President of Muslim League Allahabad session Dec 1930 — pioneered idea of a separate Muslim-majority homeland in North-West India (later developed into Pakistan demand). Wrote "Saare Jahan Se Achha" (1904) before his ideological shift. Spiritual influence on Jinnah's later communal politics. Died April 1938 before formal Pakistan Resolution.

nodes.label: Iqbal's Allahabad Address (Dec 1930)
nodes.detail: 29 December 1930 — Muhammad Iqbal's presidential address at Allahabad Muslim League session. First authoritative call for consolidating "the North-West Indian Muslims into a single State" (Punjab, NWFP, Sindh, Balochistan). Framed as self-determination within or outside British Empire. Early intellectual foundation of what became the Pakistan demand (1940 Lahore Resolution).

nodes.label: Choudhry Rahmat Ali & Pakistan Name (1933)
nodes.detail: Cambridge student who coined the acronym "Pakistan" in his 1933 pamphlet "Now or Never: Are We to Live or Perish Forever?" (later expanded 1935). P = Punjab, A = Afghania (NWFP), K = Kashmir, I = Iran-imperial?, S = Sindh, tan = Balochistan. Separately invented on ideological grounds, only later adopted by Muslim League after Lahore Resolution 1940.

nodes.label: Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution (23 March 1940)
nodes.detail: Annual Muslim League session at Minto Park, Lahore, 22-24 March 1940. Resolution moved by A.K. Fazlul Huq on 23 March — demanded that "geographically contiguous units" where Muslims were in majority be grouped to constitute "independent states" with autonomous sovereign units. Adopted by majority League delegates. Foundational demand of Pakistan. 23 March commemorated in Pakistan as Pakistan Day / Resolution Day. Hist_lahore_resolution_1940 already in working set with broader framing.

nodes.label: Direct Action Day Call (July 1946)
nodes.detail: 29 July 1946 — Muslim League Council rejected Cabinet Mission Plan and announced Direct Action to achieve Pakistan. Jinnah: "We bid good-bye to constitutional methods... Today we have also forged a pistol and are in a position to use it." 16 August 1946 declared Direct Action Day. Triggered Calcutta Killings 16-19 Aug 1946.

nodes.label: Congress Ministries Resignation (Oct-Nov 1939)
nodes.detail: Oct-Nov 1939 — Viceroy Linlithgow's 17 October statement refused to define British war aims or commit to Indian freedom. Exploited Hindu-Muslim differences, recognised Muslim League as Congress counterweight. Congress Working Committee (23 October) rejected Viceregal statement and ordered Congress provincial ministries to resign. Ended 28-month experiment of Congress Raj. League's Jinnah celebrated 22 December 1939 as "Deliverance Day" — Muslims celebrated release from "tyranny" of Congress rule.

nodes.label: Ramgarh Congress Session (March 1940)
nodes.detail: March 1940 — Maulana Azad presided. Resolution confirmed "complete independence" as only acceptable goal. Deferred civil disobedience to "when Congress organisation is considered fit enough for the purpose". Bose (Forward Bloc) held parallel "Anti-Compromise Conference" at Ramgarh demanding immediate struggle. Marked Congress-Forward Bloc ideological split.

nodes.label: August Offer (Aug 1940)
nodes.detail: 8 August 1940 — Linlithgow's offer: promise of Dominion Status after war, expansion of Executive Council with more Indians, War Advisory Council. Crucially gave Muslim League the veto — "no constitutional change without consent of minorities". Congress rejected (AICC September 1940). League welcomed effective veto. Congress responded with Individual Satyagraha.

nodes.label: Individual Satyagraha (Oct 1940 - Dec 1941)
nodes.detail: Launched 17 October 1940. Non-mass, selective protest: designated Satyagrahis publicly declared anti-war stance ("It is wrong to help British war effort with men or money") and informed District Magistrate of speech. Vinoba Bhave was first satyagrahi; Nehru the second (3 days rigorous imprisonment, later extended). Later "Delhi Chalo" trek. By May 1941 over 25,000 convicted. Dual purpose: express anti-war feeling and give British another chance to concede; also prepare Congress organisation for bigger struggle.

nodes.label: Vinoba Bhave
nodes.detail: Acharya Vinoba Bhave. Gandhian scholar from Maharashtra. Chosen by Gandhi as first Individual Satyagrahi, 17 October 1940 at Paunar (Wardha). Sanskrit scholar, founder of Bhoodan (land gift) movement 1951 — walked over 58,000 km collecting land for landless. Post-independence spiritual-social reformer.

nodes.label: Cripps Mission Details (March-April 1942)
nodes.detail: March 1942 — under US/Chinese/Labour pressure after Japanese invasion of Burma (Rangoon fell March 1942), Churchill sent Stafford Cripps to Delhi. Draft Declaration offered: Dominion Status after war, constitution-making body elected by provincial legislatures + nominated by princes, right of any province not accepting to sign separate agreement (first time Pakistan option implicit), interim British control of Defence. Congress rejected — Dominion Status not independence, Pakistan implicit, no real power transfer. Viceroy Linlithgow, Churchill, Amery all sabotaged Cripps. Gandhi called it a "post-dated cheque on a crashing bank".

nodes.label: Sir Stafford Cripps
nodes.detail: British Labour Party leader. Former friend of Nehru (since Brussels 1927). Sent by Churchill March 1942 to negotiate with Congress (Cripps Mission). Failed. Returned to India as part of Cabinet Mission 1946. Later held Chancellor of Exchequer in Attlee government.

nodes.label: Gowalia Tank (AICC Aug 1942)
nodes.detail: AICC at Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay, 7-8 August 1942. Passed Quit India Resolution 8 August. Gandhi's famous "Do or Die" speech: "The mantra is Do or Die. We shall either free India or die in the attempt; we shall not live to see the perpetuation of our slavery". Specific instructions: government servants to declare allegiance to Congress but not resign; soldiers to refuse firing on compatriots; princes to accept their people's sovereignty. Next day (9 Aug) all Congress leaders arrested. Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted Congress flag at the Tank on 9 August 1942. The ground became August Kranti Maidan.

nodes.label: Aruna Asaf Ali
nodes.detail: "Grand Old Lady of Independence Movement". Hoisted the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank on 9 August 1942 after leaders' arrests. Went underground during Quit India, edited Inquilab journal. Jailed for 7 years. Leader of 1942 underground with Achyut Patwardhan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Sucheta Kripalani. Married Asaf Ali, Congress lawyer.

nodes.label: Ram Manohar Lohia
nodes.detail: Congress Socialist leader, jail escapee with Jayaprakash Narayan (Hazaribagh Nov 1942). Led Congress Radio broadcasts from underground. Later founded Samyukta Socialist Party. Intellectual architect of non-Congress socialism post-1947.

nodes.label: Sucheta Kripalani
nodes.detail: Underground leader of Quit India in Delhi and elsewhere. Member Constituent Assembly. Sang "Vande Mataram" and "Sare Jahan Se Achha" at the Constituent Assembly's midnight session on 14-15 August 1947. Later Chief Minister of UP (1963-67) — India's first female CM.

nodes.label: Congress Radio (Usha Mehta, 1942)
nodes.detail: Clandestine Congress Radio operated by 22-year-old Usha Mehta and others (including Vithaldas Khakhar, Chandrakant Jhaveri, Vithalbhai Jhaveri) during Quit India. Broadcasts began 27 August 1942 from Bombay; ran till November 1942 when police seized the equipment. Range reached Madras. Read out news, Congress bulletins, Gandhi's messages. Ram Manohar Lohia regularly broadcast. Usha Mehta imprisoned 4 years.

nodes.label: Parallel Governments of 1942
nodes.detail: Three major "swaraj" parallel governments emerged during Quit India: (1) Ballia (East UP, August 1942) under Chittu Pande — forced collector to hand over power, released arrested Congressmen; crushed within a week; (2) Tamluk Jatiya Sarkar (Midnapore Bengal, 17 Dec 1942 - Sept 1944) — cyclone relief, schools, arbitration courts, Vidyut Vahini armed wing, paddy redistribution; (3) Satara Prati Sarkar (Maharashtra, 1943-45) under Nana Patil — longest-lasting, effective parallel authority for nearly 2 years.

nodes.label: Nana Patil + Satara Prati Sarkar
nodes.detail: Leader of Satara (Maharashtra) Prati Sarkar 1943-45. Kranti Simha ("Revolution Lion") nickname. Organised Tufani Sena and nyayadan mandals (people's courts). Anti-moneylender peasant politics. Provided parallel governance for 2 years during Quit India underground. Later joined CPI; elected to Lok Sabha 1957.

nodes.label: Gandhi's 21-Day Fast (Feb-March 1943)
nodes.detail: 10 February - 3 March 1943 — Gandhi's 21-day fast in Aga Khan Palace Poona against government's demand that he condemn Quit India violence. Gandhi refused, held government responsible for "leonine violence". Three Indian members of Viceroy's Executive Council (M.S. Aney, N.R. Sarkar, H.P. Mody) resigned. Wavell refused release, made plans for Gandhi's funeral. Gandhi survived. International solidarity from US, British Communist Party, Women's International League, Australian Council of Trade Unions. Moral defeat for the Raj.

nodes.label: Rash Behari Bose + Indian Independence League (1942)
nodes.detail: Veteran revolutionary (associated with Hardinge Bomb attempt 1912). Escaped to Japan 1915. Founded Indian Independence League at Tokyo Conference March-June 1942 — co-ordinating body of Indian nationalists in Japan-occupied SE Asia. First Supreme Commander of the Indian National Army (INA) formed in Aug-Sept 1942 under Mohan Singh. Handed over to Subhas Bose at Singapore 4 July 1943. Died 21 January 1945.

nodes.label: Mohan Singh + First INA (1942)
nodes.detail: Captain Mohan Singh (1909-1989). Captured by Japanese at Singapore Feb 1942; became first Commander of INA formed from Indian POWs Sept 1942. Disagreed with Japanese over INA's role; arrested by Japanese Dec 1942, INA disbanded. Second INA revived under S.C. Bose 1943. Post-independence joined Congress, elected to Rajya Sabha.

nodes.label: Azad Hind Government (Oct 1943)
nodes.detail: 21 October 1943 — S.C. Bose proclaimed the Provisional Government of Azad Hind (Free India) at Singapore. Cabinet: Bose (Head of State, PM, Minister of War and Foreign Affairs), Captain Lakshmi Sahgal (Minister of Women's Organisation), A.C. Chatterjee (Finance), S.A. Ayer (Publicity). Recognised by Japan, Germany, Italy, Thailand, Burma, Croatia, Manchukuo, Philippines (Japanese satellites). Headquarters moved to Rangoon. Declared war on Britain and US.

nodes.label: Rani of Jhansi Regiment
nodes.detail: Women's armed regiment of INA formed 1943 at Singapore, named after Rani Lakshmibai. Commanded by Captain Lakshmi Sahgal (Lakshmi Swaminathan). Drew recruits from Tamil, Malayali, Bengali Indian diaspora in Malaya-Singapore. Deployed in Burma Imphal-Kohima campaigns. Rare instance of women's armed combat in modern Indian history.

nodes.label: Captain Lakshmi Sahgal
nodes.detail: Dr Lakshmi Swaminathan (Lakshmi Sahgal, 1914-2012). Recruited as doctor in Singapore 1940. Joined INA 1943 on Bose's arrival. Commander of Rani of Jhansi Regiment. Minister for Women in Azad Hind Government. Captured May 1945, released 1946. Later CPM, ran for President of India 2002.

nodes.label: Battles of Imphal-Kohima (March-July 1944)
nodes.detail: March-July 1944 — INA + Japanese attempted to march on Imphal and Kohima into British India. Slogan "Chalo Delhi". Bose hoisted Azad Hind flag on Indian soil at Moirang, Manipur in April 1944. British-Indian 14th Army under Slim held and then repulsed; INA suffered heavy losses from disease, hunger, British air superiority. Turning point after which INA retreated. Marked the limit of Axis eastward advance.

nodes.label: INA Red Fort Trials (Nov 1945-Jan 1946)
nodes.detail: First trial (from 5 November 1945) at Red Fort of the three senior-most captured INA officers: Shah Nawaz Khan (Muslim), Prem Kumar Sahgal (Hindu), and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon (Sikh). Cross-communal composition turned trial into pan-Indian symbol of unity. Defence team: Bhulabhai Desai (lead), Tej Bahadur Sapru, K.N. Katju, Nehru, Asaf Ali. All three found guilty of "waging war against the King"; sentenced to transportation for life but sentences commuted by Auchinleck under political pressure and released. Sparked INA Day (12 Nov 1945), INA Week (5-11 Nov), massive popular sympathy.

nodes.label: Shah Nawaz Khan
nodes.detail: Major General in INA; led INA Division into Imphal campaign. One of three tried at Red Fort Nov 1945. Post-independence joined Congress, elected to Lok Sabha (four terms), Union Minister.

nodes.label: Prem Kumar Sahgal
nodes.detail: Military Secretary to Subhas Bose in Azad Hind Government. One of three tried at Red Fort Nov 1945. Married Captain Lakshmi Sahgal (commander of Rani of Jhansi Regiment).

nodes.label: Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon
nodes.detail: INA officer, one of three tried at Red Fort Nov 1945. Represented Sikhs in the cross-communal INA Trials trinity (with Muslim Shah Nawaz Khan and Hindu P.K. Sahgal).

nodes.label: Bhulabhai Desai + Liaqat-Desai Pact
nodes.detail: Congress lawyer. Led defence at INA Red Fort Trials Nov 1945. Negotiated Liaqat-Desai Pact 1945 with Muslim League's Liaqat Ali Khan — proposed equal Hindu-Muslim representation in interim government + 20% for minorities. Congress leaders (in jail) repudiated it. Precursor to later Cabinet Mission negotiations.

nodes.label: Wavell Plan + Simla Conference (June 1945)
nodes.detail: June 1945 — Viceroy Wavell's plan for reconstituted Executive Council with equal Hindu and Muslim representation (excluding Viceroy and C-in-C). Simla Conference 25 June - 14 July 1945 brought 21 Indian leaders together including the released Congress Working Committee and Muslim League. Failed over Jinnah's insistence that only the League could nominate Muslims (Congress insisted on nominating nationalist Muslims like Azad). Conference collapsed July 1945. First major post-war political initiative and first major failure at Congress-League unity.

nodes.label: 1945-46 Central + Provincial Elections
nodes.detail: Dec 1945 Central Legislative Assembly elections + Feb 1946 Provincial Assembly elections. Congress won 57 of 102 Central seats contested and swept non-Muslim seats (91.3%). Muslim League won all 30 Muslim seats at Centre and 427 of 509 Muslim provincial seats (hence claimed sole Muslim representation). Congress took majority in 8 of 11 provinces. INA agitation and 1942 repression were key campaign issues. Established League's electoral credential and hardened communal lines. Basis for subsequent Cabinet Mission invitation.

nodes.label: Royal Indian Navy Mutiny (Feb 1946)
nodes.detail: 18-23 February 1946 — revolt of RIN ratings against racial discrimination, bad food, after arrest of B.C. Dutt for scrawling "Quit India" on HMIS Talwar. Spread from HMIS Talwar Bombay to Castle & Fort Barracks, then HMIS Hindustan Karachi and 77 other ships/shore establishments (20,000 ratings, 78 ships). Congress flags hoisted with League and CPI flags briefly. Bombay hartal by 200,000-300,000 workers Feb 22, barricades, 228 civilians killed in police/army action, 1046 injured. Patel and Jinnah separately advised ratings to surrender. Revolt ended Feb 23. Liberating effect on anti-British sentiment but demonstrated colonial state could still repress.

nodes.label: INA Day + INA Week (Nov 1945)
nodes.detail: 12 November 1945 observed as INA Day. 5-11 November 1945 as INA Week. Massive nationwide mobilisation for release of INA prisoners during Red Fort Trial. Deshapriya Park Calcutta mass rally drew 200,000-500,000. INA Relief & Enquiry Committee formed under Congress. Sarat Chandra Bose (SC Bose's brother) led public campaign. Communal unity rare — Gurdwara donations, film stars, municipal funds, Calcutta tongawallas all contributed.

nodes.label: Cabinet Mission Plan (May 1946)
nodes.detail: Cabinet Mission (Stafford Cripps, Pethick-Lawrence, A.V. Alexander) arrived Delhi 24 March 1946. Plan announced 16 May 1946. Rejected Pakistan demand but proposed three-tier federal structure: (1) Union Centre handling Defence/External Affairs/Communications; (2) Three groups — A (Hindu-majority), B (Muslim-majority NW), C (Bengal+Assam); (3) Provinces with residuary powers. Provinces could opt out of groups after first election. Interim government envisaged. League accepted 6 June. Congress accepted with reservations on grouping compulsion. Nehru's Bombay press conference 10 July made the mission unraveled. League withdrew and called Direct Action Day.

nodes.label: Interim Government (Sept 1946)
nodes.detail: Constituted 2 September 1946 with Nehru as de facto Prime Minister (Vice President of Executive Council). Initially Congress-only; League joined 26 October 1946 after Direct Action Day violence. Liaqat Ali Khan as Finance Minister obstructed — "budget of revenge" Feb 1947 targeted capitalists; unworkable coalition. League repeatedly undermined governmental functioning from within. Persuaded Congress that only Partition would permit functional government.

nodes.label: Attlee's February 1947 Statement
nodes.detail: 20 February 1947 — British PM Clement Attlee announced in House of Commons that the British would transfer power "not later than June 1948" and Lord Louis Mountbatten would replace Wavell as Viceroy. Definite deadline concentrated minds. Radically changed the dynamics — forced Congress to decide between partition and chaos. Mountbatten arrived India 22 March 1947.

nodes.label: Indian Independence Act (July 1947)
nodes.detail: 18 July 1947 — British Parliament passed the Act. Provided for partition of British India into two Dominions: India and Pakistan, effective 15 August 1947. Each Dominion would have its own Constituent Assembly with full sovereign powers. British paramountcy over princely states to lapse (states free to accede to either Dominion). Governor-General for each Dominion (Mountbatten became first GG of India; Jinnah of Pakistan). 1935 Act to apply in modified form until new constitutions framed. Legal basis of Partition.

nodes.label: Radcliffe Boundary Commission (July 1947)
nodes.detail: Set up 30 June 1947 under Sir Cyril Radcliffe (London barrister who had never visited India) to demarcate Punjab and Bengal partition lines. Had six-week mandate, never set foot outside of Delhi simla estate. Radcliffe Award published 17 August 1947 (two days after Independence). Lines split villages, homes, irrigation systems. Responsible for chaos of 14-15 million refugee flows and 1-2 million killings of Partition.

nodes.label: Tryst with Destiny (Aug 14-15, 1947)
nodes.detail: At midnight 14-15 August 1947 — Jawaharlal Nehru's address to Constituent Assembly declaring independence: "Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny, and now the time comes when we shall redeem our pledge... At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom." Among foundational speeches of the Republic. Sucheta Kripalani sang "Vande Mataram" and "Sare Jahan Se Achha". Gandhi was in Calcutta leading peace walks, not present at celebrations.

nodes.label: Gandhi's Peace Walks (Oct 1946 - Jan 1948)
nodes.detail: November 1946 - March 1947 — Gandhi walked through Noakhali villages after October 1946 riots, barefoot, for months, restoring Muslim-Hindu confidence. Then walked through Bihar after Oct-Nov 1946 Hindu mobs massacred Muslims. Stayed in Calcutta Aug 1947 during communal tensions — his one-man peace work was more effective than multiple army brigades. Assassinated 30 January 1948 at Birla House Delhi by Nathuram Godse over Gandhi's stand on communal reconciliation.

nodes.label: Bengal School of Art
nodes.detail: Anti-academic, swadeshi-era art movement founded by Abanindranath Tagore (student of Ernest Binfield Havell). Rejected Western academic realism in favour of "revival" of Mughal/Rajput miniature traditions, Pahari, Ajanta frescoes. Centred in Calcutta's Government School of Art and from 1918 expanded to Santiniketan Kala Bhavan. Major figures: Nandalal Bose, Asit Kumar Haldar, Kshitindranath Majumdar, Jamini Roy, Mukul Dey. Famous works: Abanindranath's "Bharat Mata" 1905, "Passing of Shah Jahan", "Ganesh Janani", "Veena Player". Shaped era-9 visual nationalism.

nodes.label: Abanindranath Tagore
nodes.detail: (1871-1951). Nephew of Rabindranath Tagore. Founder of Bengal School of Art and Indian Society of Oriental Art (1907). Principal of Calcutta Government School of Art. Revived Indian traditional idioms against Western academic realism. "Bharat Mata" (1905) became a national-movement icon. Taught a generation including Nandalal Bose. Also children's author under pseudonym "Aban Thakur".

nodes.label: Nandalal Bose
nodes.detail: (1882-1966). Student of Abanindranath Tagore. Principal of Kala Bhavan Santiniketan 1922-51. Pioneered "contextual modernism" in Indian art. Painted the "Haripura Panels" for 1938 Haripura Congress Session — Santiniketan-style depictions of Indian rural life. Later designed illustrations for the Indian Constitution manuscript (1949-50). Awarded Padma Vibhushan 1954.

nodes.label: Jamini Roy
nodes.detail: (1887-1972). Student of Abanindranath Tagore at Government College of Art. Pioneered Indian modern art rooted in Kalighat patua, Bengal folk and tribal art traditions. "Mother and Child", "Krishna and Radha Dancing", "Makara". Awarded Padma Bhushan 1955. His anti-elitist mass-marketed affordable paintings democratised art.

nodes.label: Kala Bhavan, Santiniketan (1919)
nodes.detail: Art school founded 1919 at Rabindranath Tagore's Santiniketan Ashram in Bolpur, Bengal. Led by Nandalal Bose (Principal 1922-51). Focus on indigenous traditions, outdoor sketching, integration with nature, folk-art immersion. Shaped the Bengal School's second generation. Rabindranath's educational-artistic vision — precursor to Visva-Bharati University 1921.

nodes.label: Visva-Bharati University (1921)
nodes.detail: Founded 23 December 1921 by Rabindranath Tagore at Santiniketan. Universalist, anti-colonial educational vision: "Yatra Visvam Bhavatyekanidam" (Where the world makes a home in a single nest). International faculty. Rural-reconstruction wing at Sriniketan (1922). Declared a central university by Act of Parliament 1951. Unique pedagogy of open-air classes, tree-shade teaching, folk-craft integration.

nodes.label: Chhayavad Movement in Hindi Poetry (1918-1937)
nodes.detail: Romantic-spiritual movement in modern Hindi poetry, 1918-1937. Four pillars ("Chhayavad ke Stambh"): Jaishankar Prasad, Suryakant Tripathi "Nirala", Sumitranandan Pant, Mahadevi Verma. Responded against objectivity of Dwivedi era with subjective lyricism, romantic idealism, nationalist undercurrents, liberation of women and the self. Prasad's "Kamayani" epic, Nirala's "Ram ki Shakti Puja", Mahadevi's "Yama" — foundational modern Hindi texts.

nodes.label: Jaishankar Prasad
nodes.detail: (1889-1937). Hindi poet, playwright, novelist. One of the "Four Pillars of Chhayavad". Epic "Kamayani" (1936) — major modern Hindi poem. Plays: Chandragupta, Skandagupta, Dhruvaswamini. Novels: Kankal, Titli, Irawati. Shaped modern Hindi literary imagination.

nodes.label: Suryakant Tripathi "Nirala"
nodes.detail: (1896-1961). Chhayavad poet. "Ram ki Shakti Puja", "Saroj Smriti" (elegy for his daughter) are landmarks. Combined Sanskrit tradition with Bengali Vaishnav mysticism and Hindi folk. Introduced free verse (chhand-mukta) in Hindi poetry. Lifelong poverty. Influential on post-independence Hindi modernism.

nodes.label: Sumitranandan Pant
nodes.detail: (1900-1977). Chhayavad pillar. Nature poetry ("Prakritivaad") — "Veena" (1927), "Pallav" (1928). Later shift to Aurobindonian spiritualism and social realism. Jnanpith Award 1968 for "Chidambara". His early Hindi free-verse shaped modern style.

nodes.label: Mahadevi Verma
nodes.detail: (1907-1987). Chhayavad poetess, "Modern Mirabai". "Yama" (Jnanpith winner), "Neer Bhari Dukh ki Badli" — mystical, melancholic poetry. Principal of Prayag Mahila Vidyapith. Active in Progressive Writers' Association. Padma Vibhushan 1988. Central woman voice of modern Hindi literature.

nodes.label: Alam Ara (First Indian Talkie, 1931)
nodes.detail: 14 March 1931 — India's first sound film, screened at Majestic Cinema, Bombay. Produced by Imperial Film Company, directed by Ardeshir Irani. Urdu-Hindi dialogue. W.M. Khan sang India's first recorded film song "De de khuda ke naam par" (Wazir Mohammed Khan). Revolutionised Indian cinema overnight; silent films extinct within two years.

nodes.label: Prabhat Film Company (1929)
nodes.detail: Major Indian film studio founded 1929 at Kolhapur by V. Shantaram, V.G. Damle, K.R. Dhaiber, S. Fattelal and S.B. Kulkarni. Moved to Pune 1933. Known for socially conscious subjects. Made "Sairandhri" (1933) — first Indian colour film (processed in Germany), "Amrit Manthan", "Sant Tukaram" (first Indian film at Venice Film Festival 1937), "Duniya Na Mane", "Aadmi". V. Shantaram's hallmark social-reformist cinema.

nodes.label: Bombay Talkies (1934)
nodes.detail: Founded 1934 by Himansu Rai and Devika Rani at Malad, Bombay. Major early studio. "Achhut Kanya" (1936) — landmark anti-untouchability film. Trained generation of actors (Ashok Kumar, Leela Chitnis, Dilip Kumar — screen debut) and directors. Franz Osten (German) was chief director. Collapsed after Himansu Rai's death 1940 and Rai-Rani estrangement.

nodes.label: New Theatres (1931)
nodes.detail: Calcutta-based film studio founded 1931 by B.N. Sircar. Centre of Bengali and Hindi cinema pioneering. Made P.C. Barua's "Devdas" (1935) — first Indian film using Studio System; "Street Singer" (1938) starring K.L. Saigal; "Mukti" (1937). Gave birth to playback singing (R.C. Boral). Training ground for directors Bimal Roy, Nitin Bose.

nodes.label: V. Shantaram
nodes.detail: (1901-1990). Rajaram Vankudre Shantaram — filmmaker, co-founded Prabhat (1929). Founded Rajkamal Kalamandir (1942). Socially committed cinema: "Amar Jyoti" (women's emancipation), "Duniya Na Mane" (widow remarriage), "Aadmi" (prostitution), later "Do Aankhen Barah Haath" (1957). Dadasaheb Phalke Award 1985. Shaped Indian social-realist film aesthetic.

nodes.label: Himansu Rai & Devika Rani
nodes.detail: Himansu Rai (1892-1940) — pioneer producer-director; Indo-German collaborations "A Throw of Dice" (1929), "Prem Sanyas/Light of Asia" (1925). Co-founded Bombay Talkies 1934. Devika Rani (1908-1994) — great-grandniece of Rabindranath Tagore; first major female Indian film star. "Karma" (1933), "Achhut Kanya" (1936). Received first Dadasaheb Phalke Award 1969.

nodes.label: Indian People's Theatre Association (IPTA, 1943)
nodes.detail: Founded 25 May 1943 at Bombay as cultural wing of Communist Party of India. First President: Prof. Hiren Mukherjee; General Secretary: Anil de Silva. Response to Bengal Famine 1943, wartime misery, fascist threat. Plays on Bengal Famine (Bijon Bhattacharya's "Nabanna"), labour struggles, anti-communalism. Key figures: Prithviraj Kapoor, Balraj Sahni, Bijon Bhattacharya, Ritwik Ghatak, Utpal Dutt, Shombhu Mitra, K.A. Abbas. Made "Dharti Ke Lal" (1946) — first major left-wing Indian film.

nodes.label: "Dharti Ke Lal" (1946)
nodes.detail: K.A. Abbas's 1946 film on Bengal Famine 1943, produced by IPTA. Based on Bijon Bhattacharya's play "Nabanna" and Krishan Chander's story "Annadata". First major socially realist Indian film. Distributed to Soviet Union — international exposure. Influenced Indian parallel cinema.

nodes.label: K.A. Abbas
nodes.detail: Khwaja Ahmad Abbas (1914-1987). Urdu-English journalist, filmmaker, columnist. IPTA founder. Directed "Dharti Ke Lal" (1946), "Munna" (1954). Scripted Raj Kapoor's films ("Awaara", "Shree 420", "Mera Naam Joker"). Weekly column "Last Page" in Blitz 1935-87 (longest-running column in Indian journalism).

nodes.label: Prithvi Theatre (1944)
nodes.detail: Founded 15 January 1944 by Prithviraj Kapoor. Travelling Hindi theatre group that toured across India with nationalist-themed plays: "Shakuntala", "Paisa", "Ahuti", "Deewar", "Pathan", "Gaddar". Plays promoted Hindu-Muslim unity and anti-colonial themes. Closed 1960 after Prithviraj's decline. Revived as permanent theatre at Juhu, Mumbai in 1978 by Shashi Kapoor and Jennifer Kendal Kapoor.

nodes.label: Bengal Famine & Cultural Response (1943-47)
nodes.detail: Cultural mobilisation around Bengal Famine of 1943 and late-war hardship. Central to IPTA's founding (1943). Bijon Bhattacharya's "Nabanna" (The New Harvest) 1944 depicted rural starvation. Zainul Abedin's unsparing sketches of Bengal famine victims (1943-44) — internationally recognised. PWA writers (Ismat Chughtai, Saadat Hasan Manto, Krishan Chander) wrote famine/Partition stories. Galvanised post-war Left cultural politics.

nodes.label: Saadat Hasan Manto
nodes.detail: (1912-1955). Urdu short-story master. Associated with Progressive Writers' Association. Wrote for All India Radio (1937-41). Scripted Bombay Talkies films. Partition stories: "Toba Tek Singh", "Khol Do", "Thanda Gosht", "Kali Shalwar" — seared images of 1947 trauma. Migrated to Lahore 1948, alcoholic, died 1955. Along with Ismat Chughtai, faced obscenity trials by colonial state for "Bu" and "Lihaaf".

nodes.label: Ismat Chughtai
nodes.detail: (1915-1991). Urdu feminist writer. Progressive Writers' Association leader. "Lihaaf" (The Quilt, 1942) faced obscenity trial in Lahore High Court 1945 for lesbian-themed content — acquitted. "Terhi Lakeer" (semi-autobiography) 1944. Her bold treatment of female sexuality made her a landmark figure of Indian feminist literature.

nodes.label: Faiz Ahmad Faiz
nodes.detail: (1911-1984). Urdu-Punjabi revolutionary poet. Member of Progressive Writers' Movement from 1936. "Naqsh-e-Faryaadi" (1941). Served in British Indian Army during WWII (anti-fascist). Post-partition moved to Pakistan; jailed in Rawalpindi Conspiracy Case 1951-55. "Hum Dekhenge" became anthem of South Asian resistance. Lenin Peace Prize 1962. Nominated for Nobel posthumously.

nodes.label: Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi
nodes.detail: (1864-1938). Hindi editor of Saraswati magazine (1903-1920). Standardiser of modern Hindi prose. "Dwivedi Yug" (1893-1918) of Hindi literature named after him. Rigorous editorial rules shaped modern Hindi grammar and prose. Key figure in Hindi-Hindustani pre-era-9 transition.

nodes.label: Kazi Nazrul Islam
nodes.detail: (1899-1976). "Rebel Poet" (Bidrohi Kobi) of Bengal. Bilingual Bengali-Urdu poet. "Bidrohi" (1922) — seminal anti-colonial poem. Edited Dhumketu (1922). Imprisoned by British 1923 for sedition. Co-founded Workers' and Peasants' Party. Close friend of Surya Sen. Symbol of Hindu-Muslim unity. Later national poet of Bangladesh. Published Langal (Bengali Marxist weekly) with Muzaffar Ahmed.

nodes.label: Harivansh Rai Bachchan
nodes.detail: (1907-2003). Hindi poet. "Madhushala" (The House of Wine, 1935) — romantic-ruminative classic. Part of Chhayavadottar period transitioning into Pragativad (progressivism). Post-indep Sahitya Akademi award, Padma Bhushan. Father of actor Amitabh Bachchan.

nodes.label: Indian People's Theatre + Communist Cultural Politics
nodes.detail: IPTA + PWA consolidation under Communist cultural umbrella 1936-47 produced the first sustained anti-imperialist mass-cultural movement in modern India. Merged Bengali nabanna theatre tradition with new Marxist politics. Covered labour strikes, famine, partition. Talents later flowered into post-1947 "parallel cinema" (Ritwik Ghatak, Bimal Roy, Kaifi Azmi, Shombhu Mitra). Left's major lasting cultural legacy.

nodes.label: Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms)
nodes.detail: Passed by British Parliament, came into force 1921. Named after Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State for India) and Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy). Key provisions: (1) Demarcated central vs provincial subjects and legislatures; (2) Introduced "Dyarchy" in provinces — transferred subjects under ministers responsible to legislature, reserved subjects under Governor's Executive Council; (3) Introduced bicameralism at Centre — Council of State (upper) + Legislative Assembly (lower); (4) Extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans; (5) Limited franchise based on property/tax/education; (6) Created High Commissioner for India in London; (7) Required 3 of 6 Viceroy's Executive Council members to be Indian; (8) Set up Public Service Commission (established 1926); (9) Separated provincial budgets; (10) Provided for statutory commission review after 10 years (which became Simon Commission 1927). Dyarchy largely failed in practice.

nodes.label: Dyarchy (1919 Provincial Government)
nodes.detail: Dual-rule (Greek "di-arche") scheme introduced by GoI Act 1919 for provincial governance 1921-1937. Divided provincial subjects into "Transferred" (education, public health, local self-government, agriculture — under Indian ministers responsible to legislature) and "Reserved" (law & order, finance, revenue, labour, irrigation — under Governor and his Executive Council, not responsible to legislature). Widely unsuccessful: ministers had no control over finance, Governors retained veto, communal electorates undercut unity. Abolished by GoI Act 1935 in favour of Provincial Autonomy.

nodes.label: Council of State + Legislative Assembly (1919)
nodes.detail: First bicameral central legislature established under GoI Act 1919, functional 1921. Upper House: Council of State (60 members, 6-year term) — designed as conservative check, narrow franchise. Lower House: Central Legislative Assembly (145 members, 3-year term) — majority directly elected. Replaced the earlier Imperial Legislative Council. Swarajists used the Assembly to create deadlocks (Motilal Nehru, Vithalbhai Patel). Both Houses continued till 1947. Precursor to Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha.

nodes.label: Central Public Service Commission (1926)
nodes.detail: Established 1926 under GoI Act 1919 provisions (Section 96C) to recruit civil servants by open competition. Chaired by Ross Barker (first Chairman). Precursor to Federal Public Service Commission (1935) and post-independence Union Public Service Commission (UPSC, 1950). Significant Indianisation mechanism — diluted European monopoly on ICS recruitment.

nodes.label: Government of India Act 1935 — Detailed Features
nodes.detail: Longest British Act of Parliament with 321 sections, 10 schedules. Key features: (1) Provided for All-India Federation of provinces + princely states (never came into being — princes did not join); (2) Three Lists — Federal (59 items), Provincial (54), Concurrent (36); residuary powers to Viceroy; (3) Abolished dyarchy in provinces, introduced "Provincial Autonomy" (1937-39); (4) Dyarchy at Centre (never operationalised); (5) Bicameralism extended to 6 provinces: Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam, UP; (6) Communal electorates extended to SCs, women, labour; (7) Abolished 1858 Council of India; (8) Extended franchise to ~10% of population; (9) Provided for Reserve Bank of India (est. 1935); (10) Federal Court (est. 1937, precursor of Supreme Court); (11) Federal + Provincial + Joint Public Service Commissions. Basis of Indian Constitution 1950 — major constitutional scaffolding.

nodes.label: Provincial Autonomy (1937)
